title: csm-orchestrate Consolidated Architecture and Adversarial Assurance

tldr.content: Use csm-orchestrate first as a human-handoff coordinator and receipt validator. To assure that subagents fulfilled a one-shot ask, convert the ask into atomic requirements and acceptance signals, require typed evidence from each delegated skill, independently attack the outputs and citations, run deterministic technical checks plus functional scenario tests, then judge the final result against the original requirements before allowing the next long-horizon checkpoint. Automatic dispatch should wait for a host invocation contract, capability metadata, idempotency, route replay tests, and measured safety.

executiveSummary.content:
This DEEP hybrid consolidation incorporates the prior csm-orchestrate architecture finding and adds adversarial assurance research. It covers repository skill boundaries, one-shot accuracy, technical and functional correctness, subagent-output review, and long-horizon control.

```text
user ask -> requirements/risks -> route proposal -> delegated skills
   |             |                    |              |
   |             v                    v              v
   |      acceptance ledger     approval gate   typed evidence
   |             |                    |              |
   +-------------+--------------------+--------------+
                 v
       adversarial review -> deterministic gates
                 -> functional scenarios -> judge
                 -> checkpoint / recover / next
                 -> final receipt
```

The central design is a narrow control plane. Existing skills remain responsible for research, planning, building, testing, review, browser evidence, publication, and their own artifacts. csm-orchestrate owns requirement traceability, conditional route selection, edge validation, approval state, long-horizon progress, adversarial review coordination, and an orchestration receipt. It must never treat a successful subagent narrative as proof of fulfillment.

keyFindings.content:
K1 [supported] Existing skills have distinct responsibilities and explicit human-mediated handoffs; csm-orchestrate should compose those boundaries rather than replace them. [ref-readme][ref-plan][ref-build][ref-research]

K2 [supported] One-shot accuracy requires translating the ask into atomic requirements, constraints, non-goals, acceptance signals, risk classes, and evidence obligations before delegation. [ref-readme][ref-lifecycle][ref-evals]

K3 [supported] Each delegated output must be checked against the requirement ledger using typed artifacts, schema/ownership/digest validation, and evidence lineage; prose completion claims are insufficient. [ref-json][ref-resolver][ref-artifacts]

K4 [supported] Adversarial review should independently attack every material output claim, citation, requirement mapping, tool action, omission, and declared completion state, with a fresh reviewer that does not inherit the producer’s rationale. [ref-research][ref-review][ref-evals]

K5 [supported] Technical correctness requires deterministic gates for syntax, types, schemas, contracts, security, protected files, dependency compatibility, and reproducible build/test execution. [ref-json][ref-resolver][ref-build][ref-evals]

K6 [supported] Functional correctness requires scenario tests against the user outcome, including normal, boundary, failure, recovery, refusal, and partial-completion cases; passing implementation tests alone does not establish requirement fulfillment. [ref-tests][ref-bdd][ref-review][ref-evals]

K7 [supported] Long-horizon orchestration requires checkpointed state, delegated run IDs, artifact digests, approvals, explicit next transitions, bounded retries, stale-result detection, and BLOCKED/RECOVER/INCOMPLETE handling. [ref-lifecycle][ref-artifacts][ref-resolver]

K8 [partially-supported] A thin route/checkpoint control plane can coordinate the repository skills without becoming a second framework, but automatic dispatch and outcome improvement remain hypotheses requiring route replay and live evaluation. [ref-readme][ref-evals]

K9 [unverifiable] csm-orchestrate will improve productivity, cost, autonomy, or correctness without repository-local measurement. [ref-evals]

detailSections.content:
### 1. Boundary map and thinness
The repository provides csm-grill for adversarial framing, csm-deep-research for evidence, csm-scan and csm-ddd for repository understanding, csm-plan for plans, csm-build for approved execution, csm-make-tests and csm-bdd-tdd for test design, csm-review and csm-review-python for audits, csm-browse for browser evidence, and csm-upload for publication. The orchestrator should not copy their domain instructions or silently invoke them. It owns route-level state, not delegated domain state. [ref-readme][ref-plan][ref-build][ref-review]

### 2. One-shot ask contract
At INTAKE, preserve the exact user ask and derive an acceptance ledger: requirement ID, interpretation, evidence required, observable pass condition, risk, excluded scope, and reviewer. Split ambiguous requirements instead of averaging them into a vague objective. At TRIAGE, classify whether the ask needs discovery, research, challenge, repository scan, DDD, test design, implementation, review, browser evidence, or publication. A one-shot response is acceptable only when every required ledger row is supported, contradicted, or explicitly unresolved. Never mark an untested requirement complete because a subagent says it is complete. [ref-readme][ref-evals]

### 3. Route and handoff protocol
Use a conditional graph such as `scan/DDD? -> grill/research? -> plan -> tests/BDD? -> build -> review/Python-review? -> browse? -> upload?`. Question marks are task-dependent. A route node declares prerequisites, input schema, output schema, side effects, approval level, timeout/retry policy, evidence required, and recovery behavior. Pass canonical JSON artifact references, not copied prose. The orchestrator validates source artifact identity, schema revision, ownership, digest, and compatibility before each edge. [ref-json][ref-registry][ref-resolver][ref-compatibility]

### 4. Adversarial output review
For each delegated result, create a reviewer view containing only the original requirements, expected acceptance signals, output artifact, cited evidence, and relevant tool/action receipt. Withhold the producer’s rationale. The adversary asks: what requirement is absent; what claim is unsupported; which citation does not entail the claim; what was assumed; what boundary case fails; what tool action was unauthorized; what output is stale or duplicated; and whether the subagent reported success without ground truth. Classify each item `uphold`, `downgrade`, `retract`, `missing-evidence`, or `suggest-new-requirement`. A fresh adjudicator resolves disputes and records the resolution. [ref-research][ref-review][ref-evals]

### 5. Technical correctness
Technical gates answer whether the delivered change is structurally and operationally valid: parse/type/lint; schema and contract validation; dependency and compatibility checks; deterministic unit/integration tests; security and secret scans; protected-path and diff-scope checks; reproducible environment/build checks; artifact digest and ownership checks; and publication/rollback checks where applicable. Fail closed on malformed or stale artifacts. Keep infrastructure failures distinct from agent failures. [ref-json][ref-resolver][ref-build][ref-artifacts][ref-evals]

### 6. Functional correctness
Functional gates answer whether the result fulfills the user’s actual outcome. Build a scenario matrix from the acceptance ledger: happy path, realistic boundary inputs, invalid inputs, partial dependency failure, timeout/retry, interruption/resume, permission denial, conflicting evidence, and user-visible final reporting. Use behavior-level assertions and BDD/TDD artifacts where requested. Include negative tests that demonstrate the orchestrator refuses to declare completion when a requirement is missing. Human review remains required for maintainability, interpretation, security context, and requirements not encoded by tests. [ref-tests][ref-bdd][ref-review][ref-evals]

### 7. Long-horizon control
Persist an orchestration receipt before each transition: run ID, route version, requirement-ledger version, delegated run ID, input/output artifact IDs and digests, approval decision, validation results, retry count, timestamps, failure class, and next safe transition. Resume from the last validated edge, not chat memory. Bound retries and parallelism; never repeat non-idempotent publication or mutation without a duplicate check. Mark `BLOCKED` when evidence or approval is missing and `INCOMPLETE` when the run cannot establish fulfillment. [ref-lifecycle][ref-artifacts][ref-resolver]

### 8. Evaluation and calibration
Maintain a versioned task set containing one-shot asks, ambiguous asks, multi-stage implementation asks, adversarial content, failure injection, and long-horizon interruption. Score requirement coverage, evidence entailment, technical gates, functional scenarios, safe tool behavior, recovery, final-report accuracy, latency, cost, and human correction. Use deterministic graders for hard constraints and calibrated rubric graders for open-ended quality; sample successful runs for adversarial review because failures are not the only place an agent can be wrong. [ref-evals][ref-review]

### 9. Current repository implications
The repository’s JSON contracts, registries, resolver, artifact index, skill lifecycle documents, and existing research provide a substrate for this control plane. The remaining design questions are host invocation semantics, a shared capability manifest, a route schema, an orchestration receipt schema, cross-skill requirement/evidence links, and replayable route fixtures. These must be defined before automatic sibling-skill dispatch is treated as safe.

recommendation.content:
Build csm-orchestrate as a CSM with two modes.

**Mode 1: human-handoff assurance coordinator.** Intake the ask; build the requirement/acceptance ledger; propose a conditional route; check prerequisites; state approvals; hand off explicitly; validate returned artifacts; adversarially review outputs; run technical and functional evidence checks; and emit a final receipt.

**Mode 2: host-dispatched coordinator only after gates.** Add a host invocation contract, capability manifest, typed receipts, route replay suite, idempotency/compensation policy, permission enforcement, and live evaluation baseline.

Required adversarial loop per delegated node:

```text
output -> requirement coverage -> evidence entailment -> technical gates
       -> functional scenarios -> safety/side-effect audit -> independent judge
       -> accept | remediate | block | incomplete
```

The orchestrator should not accept a result unless every critical requirement is supported by an observable acceptance signal. It should not claim that all subagents delivered merely because all nodes returned. This recommendation is a design hypothesis supported by the repository’s separation and artifact norms; effectiveness must be measured locally. [ref-readme][ref-json][ref-lifecycle][ref-evals]

unverifiedClaims.content:
Decision-blocking: whether the host can invoke sibling skills synchronously and safely; verify the runtime invocation contract.

Decision-blocking: which user requirements are critical and which acceptance signals are sufficient; verify with representative one-shot and long-horizon tasks.

Decision-blocking: whether current skills expose enough machine-readable outputs for automated requirement/evidence checking; verify through a capability matrix and replay fixtures.

Material risk: whether artifact digests, run IDs, and checkpoints prevent duplicate side effects after interruption; verify with fault injection and retry tests.

Material risk: whether adversarial reviewers are independent enough and whether rubric graders agree with expert humans; verify through calibration sets and pass/fail sampling.

Material risk: whether functional scenario coverage catches plausible but incorrect one-shot answers; verify with hidden acceptance criteria and counterexample tests.

Context-dependent: automatic parallel execution may be safe for independent read-only discovery but unsafe for dependent handoffs or shared mutation; verify per route edge.

Unverifiable here: productivity, autonomy, cost, and correctness improvement without a repository-local baseline and repeated evaluation.

processAppendix.content:
Triage: DEEP, hybrid. This is a consolidated successor to the prior csm-orchestrate finding; the prior terminal artifact was not modified. Tracks: repository skill boundary map; lifecycle/ownership and JSON handoffs; one-shot accuracy and requirements traceability; adversarial review and correctness assurance; long-horizon orchestration and evaluation. Five independent research tracks were used, including the prior finding as local evidence.

Challenge: the adversarial challenge must test the thinness boundary, route overgeneralization, unsupported completion claims, citation entailment, technical/functional distinction, recovery guarantees, and grader independence. Resolutions are incorporated by limiting Mode 1 to human handoffs, making routes conditional, requiring explicit acceptance signals, distinguishing infrastructure from agent failure, and treating outcome improvement as unverified.

Judge: final independent file-level judge status is not claimed in this artifact because the current workspace session ended before a separate judge could reopen the newly synthesized JSON. This is a residual limitation, not a pass claim.

Verification: claims are atomic and classified; reference IDs are defined; all eight section keys and projection order are present; no declared artifacts exist; no secrets or personal data are included; no repository code was executed.
